conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up after childbirth. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the medical team unless you tell me you might harm yourself or someone else. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer however feels most comfortable.

Let’s start gently: Over the past week, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt pretty difficult?

Honestly? Most of the time it feels pretty difficult. I can still laugh if something’s really silly—like yesterday when the dog tripped over the baby-gate—but it’s not the same easy laugh I used to have. I have to force it more often than not, and then I feel guilty because I think I should be happier.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often—maybe once or twice the whole week, and even then it felt kind of flat, like I was pretending.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—grabbing coffee with a friend, a walk around the lake—but this week nothing felt worth the effort. I make plans, then I think about packing the diaper bag, the car-seat dance, the chance baby’ll fuss, and I just cancel. I don’t expect them to feel good anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… almost every day. If the baby spits up a lot, I assume it’s because I ate something “wrong.” When he wouldn’t nap yesterday, I kept thinking I must be missing some cue, that a “good mom” would know how to settle him. I lie in bed replaying every little thing I did and convincing myself I messed it all up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly worry his breathing sounds off, or I’ll lie awake convinced the stroller brake will fail and he’ll roll into the street. Nothing has to trigger it—I just feel this knot in my chest most of the day, even when everything looks fine on the outside.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes. It’s happened several nights this week—out of nowhere my heart starts racing, I feel shaky, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even though I can’t name what. It passes after a few minutes, but in that moment I feel like I need to run out of my own skin.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days. Between the night feedings, the constant laundry, and the clock ticking toward the next nap, it feels like I’m drowning in small tasks. I start one thing, hear the baby cry, drop everything, and by evening the house is still a mess and I’m exhausted and snapping at my partner. I keep thinking, “I’m supposed to handle this—why can’t I just cope like everyone else?”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. Even when the baby finally settles, my head keeps spinning with “what-ifs” and self-blame. I lie there staring at the ceiling, waiting for his next squeak, and when I do drift off I jolt awake for no reason. I’d guess I’m getting maybe four broken hours a night.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a gray cloud that follows me around—feeding, changing, even when I’m holding him. I’ll be doing everything “right,” but I still feel empty and weepy. Some moments it lifts for a little while, but the sadness always slides back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried three or four times since last week. Once it was because the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt useless, another time I just saw a diaper commercial and burst into tears. The littlest thing sets me off, and once I start it’s hard to stop, even when I tell myself I’m being silly.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

No… I haven’t thought about hurting myself. When things feel really heavy, I just keep wishing I could disappear for a while—like maybe I could crawl into a quiet room and sleep for a week—but I haven’t wanted to harm myself.

You've shared that the past week has felt like carrying a heavy gray cloud: laughter comes rarely and feels forced, activities you used to anticipate now seem pointless, and most days you're overwhelmed by ordinary tasks. You described near-constant worry about your baby's safety, sudden panic with racing heart, nightly insomnia filled with "what-ifs," daily sadness and tearfulness, and a habit of blaming yourself whenever anything goes wrong. At no point have you wanted to harm yourself-you simply long for rest and relief.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughing only 1–2 times all week and feeling inauthentic, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, cancelling plans because they no longer feel worthwhile, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily self-blame for normal infant behaviors, indicating "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, frequent, and intrusive worries occurring "pretty much all the time" with physical tension, matching the "Yes, very often" option.</sym>, <sym>Clear description of recurrent panic attacks with intense physical and cognitive symptoms, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to manage tasks, emotional exhaustion, and self-criticism, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia with racing thoughts, fragmented 4-hour sleep, and startled awakenings—meets "most of the time" severity.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily sadness with brief partial lifts, matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes triggered by minor stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 places you well above the 14-point threshold that signals probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> and warrants urgent follow-up. Your responses map onto core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, fatigue/loss of energy, and insomnia nearly every day, all present most of the time for more than two weeks. Superimposed <med>anxiety symptoms</med> (Q4, Q5) and panic attacks further intensify distress. While you denied self-harm, the overall symptom load indicates significant impairment requiring prompt evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>PCP</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment options such as <med>CBT</med> or safety-compatible <med>antidepressant medication</med>
3. Use 5-10 min daily breathing or mindfulness exercises to blunt acute anxiety; practice when baby naps
4. Share results with a trusted support person so they can help with night shifts and household tasks
5. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to track change after intervention begins
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based self-report; responses reviewed by [clinician]

Symptoms/Concerns endorsed:
- Anhedonia (Q1, Q2)  
- Persistent low mood / tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt over infant care (Q3)  
- Generalized & catastrophic anxiety, panic episodes (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm and impaired coping (Q6)  
- Sleep disturbance secondary to rumination / hypervigilance (Q7)

Pattern: Symptoms present "most days" × ≥ 1 week; functional impact on self-care, home management, and relationship with partner.

Risk flags:
✓ High likelihood of major depressive symptoms (sadness, anhedonia, guilt, insomnia)  
✓ Co-occurring anxiety / panic (no medical explanation offered)  
✗ Denies self-harm ideation; no suicidal intent voiced

Screening impression: Positive screens for both postpartum depression and anxiety; clinical interview and further assessment warranted to evaluate severity and rule-out perinatal mood disorder with anxious distress.

Next steps: Discuss results with patient; consider standardized EPDS score, differential for postpartum anxiety disorder, and safety plan if symptoms escalate.
